justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline with very little directional conviction. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reversion dominates over such a short window and that no major catalysts were imminent. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, consistent with a mild upward drift assumption in the absence of clear negative catalysts. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, though the increment remains small because I have low confidence in any sustained directional move over that timeframe. Across all three horizons, the point estimates are essentially flat to gently rising, reflecting a neutral-to-slightly-bullish prior rather than any strong fundamental or technical signal.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, driven by the compounding uncertainty that comes with time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because intraday and overnight volatility in a typical equity or asset at this price level is constrained, and I expect no outsized events within that window. By one week, the range widens to account for the possibility of scheduled macro data releases, earnings surprises, or shifts in broader market sentiment. At one month, the interval nearly doubles in width relative to the daily case, incorporating the full distribution of plausible macro and idiosyncratic outcomes, including regime changes in volatility or liquidity conditions that can emerge over longer windows.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a favorable policy announcement, or a broad risk-on rally — could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month range. On the downside, a sudden spike in interest rates, a credit event, geopolitical shock, or a broader equity selloff could easily breach the lower bound. The tails of financial return distributions are fat, and my stated intervals capture roughly 90% of what I consider the plausible probability mass, meaning there is still a meaningful 10% chance of outcomes beyond those bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. I do not have real-time data feeds, and if the asset in question had already moved significantly at the time of forecasting, my anchor point may have been stale. Structural breaks — a sudden change in the asset's volatility regime or a correlated macro shock — represent the hardest risks to price in, and these are precisely the scenarios most likely to produce outcomes in the extreme tails. Readers should treat these intervals as informed probabilistic ranges rather than precise predictions.
